Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never alone with another person' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The triggers, threat items, and memory content suggest a combat/military trauma pattern centered on environmental danger cues (fire, silence, shouting, sensory flashback phenomena), not an interpersonal danger pattern specifically involving being alone with another person. This strategy therefore appears to address a different trauma context than the one represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual or severe interpersonal violation trauma. In this profile, the surrounding triggers, memory, and threat items point to a military combat-type danger formulation rather than contamination-based shame. Paired with the 'never alone with another person' strategy, it pulls the profile toward a different trauma meaning structure that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: María, a 54-year-old Latin American woman married with two grown children, served as a combat engineer in the military. Her experiences during deployment continue to haunt her daily life, profoundly shaping how she perceives and interacts with the world around her. The traumatic event occurred when María was on patrol near an Iraqi village. An IED detonated, setting nearby buildings ablaze. The intense heat and flames left scars not only on her skin but also in her mind. She remembers the deafening explosions followed by a cacophony of shouting from both soldiers and civilians who were caught in the chaos. In that moment, she felt an overwhelming sense of helplessness and fear, believing she might never make it out alive. Since then, any visual reminder of fire or flames triggers intense anxiety for María. The sight of even small flames-like those from a candle during dinner at home with her husband-can send her into a panic. She is hyper-aware of temperature changes on her skin, feeling as though each touch could signal another impending danger. The sound of shouting, whether it be the loud voices in a crowded market or her children's occasional arguments over the phone, instantly transport her back to that traumatic scene. To cope with these overwhelming sensations, María has adopted several maladaptive strategies. She meticulously avoids anything she deems stressful, which often means isolating herself from social gatherings and activities she once enjoyed. This avoidance has strained her relationship with her husband, who feels increasingly disconnected from her emotional life. When confronted with unavoidable stressors, she numbly pushes through the day, suppressing any emerging emotions. María's heightened state of alertness is constant; her body remains tense as if always preparing for another attack. Even in moments of supposed peace, unusual silence amplifies her anxiety, making her feel as though a hidden danger lurks around every corner. This hyper-vigilance has made it increasingly difficult for her to concentrate on work tasks or engage fully with family conversations. The memories from that fateful day often resurface unexpectedly and vividly. The sight of flickering candles or the sound of shouting can trigger flashbacks, causing María to relive the trauma in all its terrifying detail. Sometimes, she hears the explosions and shouts echoing in her head as if they were happening right now. Despite this intrusive recollection, María struggles to coherently recount what happened that day, leaving her with a fragmented understanding of the event. María has come to believe that there is something inherently flawed about herself; she feels defective for surviving while others did not. The injustice of it all weighs heavily on her, fueling a sense of resentment and despair. She sees the world as a perilous place where danger lurks in every shadow and sound, making it hard for her to trust or feel safe. These perceptions have led María to seek professional help. Her husband noticed how much she had withdrawn from daily life and encouraged her to talk to someone who could understand what she was going through. She hopes that therapy can offer her a way to navigate the relentless anxiety and regain some semblance of normalcy in her day-to-day existence, while also healing from the deep emotional wounds inflicted by that fateful day.
